title: Astronaut
tagline: Ride a rocket, float above the world, and come home to tell the story.

stars.name: Gravity & Orbits
stars.pretest: Fire a cannonball sideways from a very tall mountain, faster and faster each time. What eventually happens?
stars.lesson: An orbit is falling that keeps missing the ground. Move sideways fast enough and Earth's surface curves away as quickly as you fall. The ISS, about 400 km up, travels roughly 7.7 km/s and circles Earth every 90 minutes or so. Gravity up there is still about 90% of what you feel on the ground. Astronauts float because they and the station are in constant free fall together, not because gravity is gone.

quiz.q: Why do astronauts on the ISS float?
options: The station spins fast enough to cancel gravity
There is no gravity at that altitude
They and the station are in continuous free fall around Earth
quiz.why: Gravity at ISS height is still about 90% of surface gravity. Everything on board falls together around Earth, so nothing pushes on anything else.

quiz.q: Roughly how fast does the ISS travel?
quiz.why: About 7.7 km/s, or roughly 28,000 km/h. That sideways speed is what keeps it from falling into the ground.

quiz.q: About how long does one ISS orbit take?
quiz.why: At about 7.7 km/s around a roughly 400 km high orbit, one lap takes about 90 minutes, so astronauts see around 16 sunrises a day.

stars.name: Rocket Propulsion
stars.pretest: Rockets work in space where there is no air to push against. So what are they pushing on?
stars.lesson: A rocket throws mass backward and gets pushed forward: Newton's third law. It needs no air, which is why rockets work in a vacuum. The rocket equation says your speed gain depends on how fast the exhaust leaves and on how much of your launch mass is fuel. Because most of a rocket is fuel, engineers use stages: drop the empty tanks, so you stop carrying dead weight.

quiz.q: What two things mainly set how much speed a rocket can gain?
options: Exhaust speed and the ratio of fueled mass to empty mass
Number of astronauts and cabin size
quiz.why: That is the rocket equation: faster exhaust and a larger fuel fraction both give more change in velocity.

quiz.q: Why do rockets use stages?
options: To look more impressive on TV
Dropping empty tanks means less mass left to accelerate
Each stage uses a different kind of air
quiz.why: Empty tanks are dead weight. Shedding them lets the remaining rocket gain speed far more efficiently.

quiz.q: A rocket engine works in the vacuum of space because...
options: It pushes against traces of air
It throws exhaust backward and is pushed forward in return
It pushes against the solar wind
It pushes against the Moon's gravity
quiz.why: Newton's third law: every action has an equal and opposite reaction. No air is needed.

stars.name: The Body in Space
stars.pretest: After six months in orbit, what part of an astronaut's body is changed the most, and why?
stars.lesson: Without gravity loading the body, bones and muscles weaken. Weight-bearing bones can lose around 1% of their density per month, so astronauts exercise about two hours a day on a treadmill, bike, and resistance machine. Body fluids shift toward the head, causing puffy faces and pressure changes that can affect eyesight. Radiation is another concern, since Earth's atmosphere no longer shields them. Recovery on Earth takes weeks to months.

quiz.q: Why do astronauts exercise about two hours every day?
options: Because it is required for docking
To counter bone and muscle loss
quiz.why: Without gravity loading the skeleton and muscles, they weaken. Daily resistance and cardio work slows that loss.

quiz.q: What happens to body fluids in microgravity?
options: They all pool in the feet
quiz.why: On Earth gravity pulls fluid toward the legs. In orbit it redistributes upward, causing puffy faces and head pressure.

quiz.q: Which bones lose density fastest in orbit?
options: Weight-bearing bones such as hips, legs, and spine
quiz.why: Bones adapt to the loads they carry. When the load disappears, the ones that normally bear the most weight lose the most.

stars.name: Orbital Maneuvers
stars.pretest: You are in orbit and want to climb to a higher orbit. Do you burn forward, backward, or straight up?
stars.lesson: To go higher, burn prograde, in the direction you are already moving. That raises the orbit on the opposite side. Counterintuitively, a higher orbit is slower, because gravity is weaker there and the path is longer. A Hohmann transfer is the efficient two-burn trip between circular orbits: one burn stretches your orbit up to the target, and a second burn at the top circularizes it. Burning retrograde, backward, lowers your orbit.

quiz.q: To raise your orbit, which direction do you burn?
quiz.why: Adding speed along your direction of travel raises the opposite side of the orbit.

quiz.q: Compared with a low orbit, a satellite in a higher circular orbit moves...
quiz.why: Gravity is weaker farther out, so less orbital speed is needed to stay up. Higher orbits are slower and take longer per lap.

quiz.q: How many burns does a Hohmann transfer between two circular orbits use?
quiz.why: One burn sets the transfer ellipse, and a second circularizes at the destination orbit.

stars.name: The Space Environment
stars.pretest: Space is famously cold. So why do spacecraft and suits need cooling systems?
stars.lesson: Space is a near-vacuum, so heat cannot be carried away by air. It leaves only as radiation. In sunlight, spacecraft surfaces can exceed 100 °C, and in shadow they can drop below -100 °C; the ISS swings between them every orbit. Radiation from the Sun and cosmic rays is another hazard. Earth's magnetic field partly shields low Earth orbit, which is one reason trips to the Moon and Mars carry more radiation risk.

quiz.q: Why is overheating a real problem for spacecraft despite the cold of space?
options: With no air, heat cannot be carried away except by radiating it
quiz.why: Without air, there is no convection. Equipment heat must be moved to radiators that emit it as infrared.

quiz.q: Why is radiation exposure higher beyond low Earth orbit?
options: It leaves the partial protection of Earth's magnetic field
quiz.why: Earth's magnetosphere deflects a lot of charged particles near the planet. Past it, crews are far more exposed.

quiz.q: How do spacecraft shed excess heat?
quiz.why: Radiators carry heat from onboard systems and emit it as infrared light, the only way to cool off in a vacuum.

stars.name: Life Support
stars.pretest: True or false: every drop of water astronauts drink has to be launched from Earth.
stars.lesson: False. The ISS recycles most of its water, including urine and moisture from breath and sweat, into drinking water, recovering well over 90%. Oxygen comes mostly from electrolysis: using electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. Scrubbers remove carbon dioxide, which builds up quickly in a sealed cabin and must be removed continuously. The cabin is held near Earth's sea-level pressure so crews can breathe normally.

quiz.q: How does the ISS mainly make oxygen?
quiz.why: Electrolysis splits water into hydrogen and oxygen. The oxygen is released into the cabin.

quiz.q: How much of the ISS's water is recycled?
options: Well over 90%, including urine and humidity
None, all of it comes from Earth
quiz.why: Water recovery systems turn urine and cabin humidity back into drinking water, cutting resupply needs dramatically.

quiz.q: Why must carbon dioxide be removed continuously?
options: It builds up quickly in a sealed cabin
It makes the cabin too cold
quiz.why: Every breath adds CO2. In a closed space it accumulates fast, so scrubbers run all the time.

stars.name: Rendezvous & Docking
stars.pretest: A station is ahead of you in the same orbit. To catch it, do you speed up or slow down?
stars.lesson: Slow down. Braking drops you into a lower orbit, where you travel faster and gain on the station; then you raise your orbit again as you close in. This is called phasing. Final approach is slow: contact speeds are only a few centimeters per second, along planned paths with go/no-go checks. Many modern spacecraft, like Crew Dragon, dock automatically while the crew monitors and can take manual control.

quiz.q: A station is ahead of you in the same orbit. To catch up you should...
options: Slow down to a lower, faster orbit
quiz.why: Burning prograde would lift you into a slower, higher orbit and you would fall behind. Dropping lower makes you gain on the target.

quiz.q: Why do lower orbits have a higher orbital speed?
options: The Moon pulls on you less
quiz.why: Stronger gravity at lower altitude requires more speed to stay in orbit.

quiz.q: How fast are two spacecraft moving toward each other at contact when docking?
quiz.why: Docking is a gentle touch, only a few centimeters per second, so hardware is not damaged and latches can engage.

stars.name: Reentry & Landing
stars.pretest: What mostly heats a capsule during reentry: friction with the air, or something else?
stars.lesson: Mostly something else. The capsule hits air so fast, about 7.8 km/s from orbit, that the air cannot get out of the way. It compresses into a shock wave in front of the vehicle, heating to thousands of degrees. Blunt shapes push that shock away from the hull. Heat shields, often ablative, char and burn away, carrying heat with them. To leave orbit, you burn retrograde to lower your path into the atmosphere.

quiz.q: What causes most of the heating during reentry?
options: Compression of air into a shock wave ahead of the vehicle
quiz.why: At orbital speed the air is compressed so violently that it becomes extremely hot, far more than simple friction would produce.

quiz.q: Why are reentry capsules blunt rather than pointy?
options: It keeps the hot shock wave away from the hull
quiz.why: A blunt body creates a shock wave that stands off from the surface, carrying most of the heat into the air instead of the hull.

quiz.q: To leave orbit and come home, you burn...
options: You do not need to burn
quiz.why: A retrograde burn lowers the far side of your orbit until it dips into the atmosphere.

stars.name: Spacewalks & Suits
stars.pretest: Why can an astronaut not just step from the station straight into a spacewalk?
stars.lesson: Suits are pressurized to roughly 30% of cabin pressure, with pure oxygen, because high pressure makes suits stiff and hard to move. But going from nitrogen-rich cabin air to low pressure can form nitrogen bubbles in the blood, the bends. So astronauts prebreathe pure oxygen for hours to flush nitrogen out. Tethers keep them attached, and training happens in giant underwater pools that mimic weightlessness.

quiz.q: Why do astronauts prebreathe pure oxygen before a spacewalk?
options: To flush nitrogen and avoid decompression sickness
quiz.why: Nitrogen dissolved in the body can form bubbles when pressure drops, just like divers' decompression sickness.

quiz.q: Why are spacesuits kept at a much lower pressure than the cabin?
options: Lower pressure makes the suit flexible enough to work in
Oxygen runs out faster at high pressure
Astronauts feel hotter at high pressure
quiz.why: A highly pressurized suit is like an inflated balloon, stiff and exhausting to bend.

quiz.q: Why do astronauts train for spacewalks in huge underwater pools?
options: It is the only way to test suits for leaks
quiz.why: Buoyancy cancels most of the weight of the suit and tools, giving a close approximation of floating.

stars.name: Mission Ready
stars.pretest: Your suit shows a minor warning in the middle of a spacewalk. What do you do first?
stars.lesson: Real missions chain every star together: launch, orbit, rendezvous, docking, work, undocking, deorbit, reentry, and recovery, each step planned and rehearsed. Safety comes from procedures and communication, not heroics. Crews use checklists and closed-loop communication: the receiver repeats the instruction back so errors get caught. Systems are redundant, because nobody can pop out for repairs. Calm, clear calls and following the plan keep problems small.

quiz.q: Which is the correct order for a typical mission?
options: Launch, rendezvous and docking, undocking, deorbit burn, reentry
quiz.why: You launch, rendezvous and dock, do your work, undock, burn to deorbit, and then enter the atmosphere.

quiz.q: Your suit shows a minor warning during a spacewalk. What is the best first response?
options: Quietly fix it with duct tape
Report it to the team and follow the procedure
quiz.why: Calling it out and following the checklist keeps everyone informed and handles problems while they are still small.

quiz.q: What is closed-loop communication?
options: The receiver repeats an instruction back to confirm it
quiz.why: Repeating the instruction back lets the sender catch misunderstandings immediately.
